mainTopic: Why a שכיר swears and collects his wages: the רבנן's תקנה, the 'busy employer' reason, and its limits
overview: The משנה says a שכיר who asks for his pay on time swears and collects. The גמרא asks why the רבנן made this unusual rule, since normally the defendant swears and goes free. First the wording of שמואל's statement is corrected from 'great הלכות' to 'great תקנות' and finally to 'fixed תקנות'. The reason given is that the oath really belonged to the בעל הבית, but the רבנן moved it to the worker because he needs his wages to live. The גמרא tries to defend this by asking who benefits economically, but that argument ends in a stalemate. So it gives a new reason: the employer is busy with many workers and may have forgotten that he did not pay. The oath is kept only to put the employer's mind at ease. Witnesses and advance payment are not practical fixes. The 'forgetting' worry does not apply to the agreed wage, which people remember. It also does not apply after the payment time, when we presume the employer did not violate בל תלין. The amud ends as the גמרא begins to explain why the employer's busyness matters only before the payment deadline, and this continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Quoting the משנה about the hired worker
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the line from the משנה: a שכיר who claims his wages on time swears and collects.
steps.simpleTranslation: A hired worker who asks for his pay at the right time swears and takes his pay, etc.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes the משנה it is about to discuss. This is a setup line for the question that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The case is a dispute: the worker says he was not paid, and the employer says he already paid. The משנה rules that the worker swears and collects. The גמרא will now ask why this is so.

keyTerms.meaning: At his proper time (when wages are due)
Swears and takes (collects money by taking an oath)

phrases.english: A hired worker, at his proper time
phrases.notes: He means a worker asking for his pay right when it is due, while the employer says, 'I already paid you.'

phrases.english: swears and takes, etc.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opening quote of the משנה
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A שכיר claiming wages on time takes an oath and collects.

steps.title: Why does the worker get to swear and collect?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why the רבנן set up a rule that the שכיר, who is the one claiming money, swears and collects.
steps.simpleTranslation: Why did the רבנן set it up so that a hired worker swears and takes his money?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks for the reason behind the משנה's rule.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally the person being sued (the defendant) swears and goes free. The one making the claim cannot collect just by swearing. Here the claimant swears and collects, so the גמרא wants to know why the רבנן made this change.

keyTerms.meaning: The Rabbis instituted (made a rabbinic enactment)

steps.confusionAlert: This rule is a תקנה, a rabbinic enactment. By basic law, the בעל הבית would swear and be exempt. Keep that in mind for the whole sugya.

phrases.english: A hired worker — why
did the Rabbis institute for him
that he should swear and take?
phrases.notes: Some versions have the word in round brackets; the word in square brackets is the corrected wording. Either way it means 'that he swears.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the reason behind the משנה just quoted
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The reason the רבנן reversed the usual oath rule and let the plaintiff swear and collect.

steps.title: שמואל: these are great הלכות
steps.stepSummary: רב יהודה quotes שמואל: the משנה is teaching 'great הלכות' here.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יהודה said in the name of שמואל: They taught great laws here.
steps.whatsHappening: רב יהודה gives a first response in the name of שמואל. He describes these rules as important הלכות.
steps.deeperAnalysis: שמואל's point is that these are special, important rules. That explains why they break the normal pattern. The גמרא will now examine his choice of words.

phrases.english: Rav Yehuda said that Shmuel said:
They taught great laws here.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה אָמַר שְׁמוּאֵל הֲלָכוֹת גְּדוֹלוֹת שָׁנוּ כָּאן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: First response to the question of step 2
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: These rules are 'great הלכות', special laws.

steps.title: These aren't הלכות, they're תקנות
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא objects to the word הלכות: these rules are rabbinic enactments, not הלכות.
steps.simpleTranslation: Are these laws? These are enactments!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the word שמואל used. A rule the רבנן set up should be called a תקנה, not a הלכה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word הלכה sounds like a basic law. But step 2 already said the רבנן instituted this rule. So the right word is תקנות, enactments.

phrases.english: Are these laws?
These are enactments!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the wording of step 3
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: These rules were instituted by the רבנן, so they are תקנות, not הלכות.

steps.title: Corrected version: great תקנות
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא changes the quote: שמואל said 'great תקנות' were taught here.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, רב יהודה said that שמואל said: They taught great enactments here.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא accepts the challenge and fixes the wording of שמואל's statement.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word הלכות is swapped for תקנות. The idea that these rules are 'great' stays the same.

phrases.aramaic: אֶלָּא אָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה אָמַר שְׁמוּאֵל:
phrases.english: Rather, Rav Yehuda said that Shmuel said:
They taught great enactments here.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא אָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה אָמַר שְׁמוּאֵל תַּקָּנוֹת גְּדוֹלוֹת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Fixes the wording that step 4 challenged
steps.terutzResolutionType: Correcting the wording of the quote

steps.title: Does 'great' mean some תקנות are small?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא objects to the word 'great': calling these תקנות great suggests that other תקנות are minor.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'Great' — does that imply there are small ones?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the corrected wording again, this time the word גדולות.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If some תקנות are 'great', it sounds like other rabbinic enactments are unimportant. The גמרא does not accept that, so the wording still needs fixing.

phrases.english: 'Great' — that implies there are small ones?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the corrected wording of step 5
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Calling some תקנות 'great' implies that other תקנות are minor, which is not acceptable.

steps.title: רב נחמן's version: fixed תקנות
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן quotes שמואל differently: these are 'fixed' תקנות.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, רב נחמן said that שמואל said: They taught fixed enactments here.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new version of שמואל's statement, from רב נחמן, that avoids the problem with 'great'.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word קבועות, 'fixed' or 'set firmly', does not suggest that other תקנות are minor. It just says these are firm, lasting enactments.

phrases.aramaic: אֶלָּא אָמַר רַב נַחְמָן אָמַר שְׁמוּאֵל:
phrases.english: Rather, Rav Nachman said that Shmuel said:
They taught fixed enactments here.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא אָמַר רַב נַחְמָן אָמַר שְׁמוּאֵל תַּקָּנוֹת קְבוּעוֹת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Resolves the challenge of step 6 with new wording
steps.terutzResolutionType: A different version of the quote from another אמורא
steps.terutzMaskana: 'Fixed תקנות', which implies nothing negative about other תקנות.

steps.title: The oath was moved from the employer to the worker
steps.stepSummary: The real reason: the oath belonged to the בעל הבית, but the רבנן moved it onto the שכיר because he needs his wages to live.
steps.simpleTranslation: The oath is really the employer's, but the רבנן took it away from the employer and put it on the hired worker, because of the worker's livelihood.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now answers the question from step 2 and explains why the worker swears and collects.
steps.deeperAnalysis: By basic law, the בעל הבית, as defendant, would swear that he paid and be exempt. The רבנן moved that oath to the שכיר so he can collect. They did this because the worker depends on his pay to survive.

keyTerms.meaning: His livelihood, what he needs to live

steps.whatToRemember: The שכיר's oath is a תקנה: the oath that would normally belong to the בעל הבית was moved onto the worker because of the worker's livelihood.
steps.whyThisMatters: This is the basic reason for the whole rule. The rest of the sugya tests whether it is fair to the employer.

phrases.english: The oath is the employer's,
but the Rabbis uprooted the employer's oath
and placed it upon the hired worker,
because of the hired worker's livelihood.

steps.triggerLanguage: שְׁבוּעָה דְּבַעַל הַבַּיִת הִיא וְעַקְרוּהָ רַבָּנַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the wording is settled, gives the reason that answers step 2
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The רבנן transferred the employer's oath to the worker because of the worker's need for his wages.

steps.title: Why should the employer lose out?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges: should the בעל הבית lose money just because the שכיר needs to make a living?
steps.simpleTranslation: And because of the worker's livelihood, should we make the employer lose?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the reason just given as unfair to the employer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The worker's need does not obviously justify taking away the employer's right to swear and be exempt. Why should one side's need cost the other side money?

phrases.english: And because of the hired worker's livelihood
should we cause a loss to the employer?
phrases.notes: Some versions have the word in round brackets; the word in square brackets is the corrected wording, 'we cause a loss.'

steps.triggerLanguage: וּמִשּׁוּם כְּדֵי חַיָּיו דְּשָׂכִיר מַפְסְדִינַן לֵיהּ לְבַעַל הַבַּיִת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the reason given in step 8
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: One party's need should not be a reason to make the other party lose money.

steps.title: The employer benefits too
steps.stepSummary: The בעל הבית himself prefers this rule, because it makes workers willing to work for him.
steps.simpleTranslation: The employer himself is happy that the worker swears and takes, so that workers will hire themselves out to him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the rule is not really a loss for the employer. It helps him find workers.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If workers know their pay is protected, they will agree to work. So the תקנה serves the employer's own interest as well as the worker's.

keyTerms.meaning: It is preferable to him, he is happy with it

phrases.english: The employer himself prefers
that the hired worker swear and take,
so that workers will hire themselves out to him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 9
steps.terutzResolutionType: Shows the rule benefits the challenged party too
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The rule is a pure loss for the בעל הבית.
steps.terutzMaskana: The rule helps the בעל הבית attract workers.

steps.title: Flip it: the worker would gain from the opposite rule
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא turns the argument around: the שכיר would also benefit if the employer swore and was exempt, because then employers would be willing to hire him.
steps.simpleTranslation: The worker himself should be happy that the employer swears and is exempt, so that the employer will hire him!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the answer by showing the same logic works in the other direction.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If rules that protect workers make workers willing to work, then rules that protect employers make employers willing to hire. So 'it benefits the other side' cannot decide whose side the תקנה should take.

phrases.english: The hired worker himself should prefer
that the employer swear and be exempt,
so that the employer will hire him?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Turns the logic of step 10 around
steps.kashyaTarget: The answer in step 10 that the employer benefits
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The same reasoning shows the worker would benefit from the opposite rule, so the reasoning proves nothing.

steps.title: The employer has to hire no matter what
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the employer must hire workers no matter what, so the worker does not need to give up his protection to get hired.
steps.simpleTranslation: Against his will he hires.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the reversal: the employer has no choice. He needs workers, so he will hire them anyway.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The two sides are not equal. The employer cannot run his business without workers. So a rule that favors workers will not stop him from hiring.

keyTerms.meaning: Against his will, he has no choice

phrases.english: He has no choice but to hire.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the reversal in step 11
steps.terutzResolutionType: Points out that the two sides are not in the same position
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The employer might refuse to hire if the rules favor workers.
steps.terutzMaskana: The employer must hire anyway, so the worker loses nothing by being protected.

steps.title: The worker also has to work no matter what
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא pushes back: the שכיר also has no choice. He must hire himself out to make a living.
steps.simpleTranslation: A hired worker too is hired against his will!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the last answer by showing the worker is also forced by need, so both sides are equal again.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the employer must hire, the worker must also work to live. So the argument from step 12 does not prove that the rule should favor the worker. In the next step the גמרא drops this whole line of reasoning and gives a new reason.

keyTerms.meaning: He is hired, hires himself out

phrases.english: A hired worker too is hired out against his will!
phrases.notes: Some versions leave out the word in round brackets; the meaning stays the same.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer of step 12
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The worker is just as forced by need as the employer, so the two sides are balanced again and the question returns.

steps.title: New reason: the employer is busy with many workers
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא drops the economic argument and explains the rule differently: the בעל הבית is busy with many workers and may have forgotten whether he paid.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, the employer is busy with many workers.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא sets aside the back-and-forth about who needs whom. It gives a brand-new reason why the שכיר gets to take a שבועה and collect.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Steps 9 to 13 tried to explain the rule by asking who benefits economically, and that argument ended in a stalemate. Now the reason is about memory: the בעל הבית deals with many workers, so he is more likely to be mistaken about paying this one. The worker only deals with one employer, so he is more likely to remember correctly.

keyTerms.meaning: Rather. Signals dropping the earlier approach for a new one.

phrases.english: Rather, the employer
is busy with many workers.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא בַּעַל הַבַּיִת טָרוּד בְּפוֹעֲלִים הוּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Abandons the economic reasoning that step 13 left stuck, and offers a reason based on who is more likely to remember.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The rule was based on economic benefit to one side.
steps.terutzMaskana: The rule is based on the likelihood that a busy employer forgot that he had not paid.

steps.title: Then why does the worker need an oath at all?
steps.stepSummary: If the בעל הבית probably forgot, the שכיר should be paid without any שבועה.
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, let him pay him without an oath!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the new reason. If we assume the employer forgot, why make the worker swear?
steps.deeperAnalysis: The new reason seems to make the worker's claim more believable than the employer's. If so, the שבועה seems unnecessary, and the worker should just collect.

keyTerms.meaning: If so. Introduces a challenge that follows from the last statement.

phrases.english: If so, let him give him his wages
without an oath!

steps.triggerLanguage: אִי הָכִי נִיתֵּב לֵיהּ בְּלָא שְׁבוּעָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the new reason given in step 14.
steps.kashyaTarget: The need for the worker's שבועה
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If the employer probably forgot, the worker's claim is strong enough to need no oath.

steps.title: The oath puts the employer's mind at ease
steps.stepSummary: The שבועה is there to calm the בעל הבית, so he does not feel cheated.
steps.simpleTranslation: In order to put the employer's mind at ease.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the oath is not needed to prove the worker is right. It is there so the employer can accept the payment calmly.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Legally, the worker's claim is strong enough. But the employer still thinks he paid. Making the worker swear reassures the employer that he is not being tricked into paying twice.

keyTerms.meaning: To calm his mind, to put him at ease.

phrases.english: In order to put the mind at ease
of the employer.

steps.triggerLanguage: כְּדֵי לְהָפִיס דַּעְתּוֹ שֶׁל בַּעַל הַבַּיִת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 15's challenge.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Explains the purpose of the law
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The oath must exist to prove the worker's claim, so if the claim is strong it would be unnecessary.
steps.terutzMaskana: The oath serves to reassure the employer, not to establish the worker's right.

steps.title: Why not pay in front of witnesses?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why the בעל הבית doesn't simply pay in front of עדים and avoid the whole doubt.
steps.simpleTranslation: But let him pay him in front of witnesses!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא suggests a simple fix: if forgetting is the problem, the employer should pay with witnesses present.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If every payment were witnessed, there would never be a question of whether the worker was paid. Then no oath and no special rule would be needed.

phrases.english: But let him give him his wages in front of witnesses?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions why the problem of forgetting isn't avoided altogether.
steps.kashyaTarget: The need for this special rule at all
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Witnessed payment would remove the doubt, so the special rule should not be needed.

steps.title: Witnesses are too much trouble
steps.stepSummary: Finding עדים for every payment is too much of a burden for both sides.
steps.simpleTranslation: The matter is a bother for them.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that bringing witnesses to every payday is a hassle for both employer and worker.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Workers are paid often, sometimes daily. Arranging witnesses each time is not realistic, so people don't do it, and the doubt remains.

phrases.english: The matter is a bother for them.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 17.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Paying with witnesses is an easy solution.
steps.terutzMaskana: It is too burdensome to be practical.

steps.title: Why not pay in advance?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why the בעל הבית doesn't pay before the work starts, when he is less busy.
steps.simpleTranslation: But let him pay him at the start!
steps.whatsHappening: Another suggested fix: pay the worker up front, before the busy workday begins, so there's nothing to forget.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The forgetting happens at the end, when the employer is busy settling with many workers. Paying at the beginning would avoid that confusion.

phrases.english: But let him give him his wages at the start?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second suggested way to avoid the doubt.
steps.kashyaTarget: The need for this special rule
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Advance payment would avoid the end-of-day confusion.

steps.title: Both sides prefer payment afterward
steps.stepSummary: Both the בעל הבית and the שכיר prefer הקפה, meaning the wages are paid later rather than up front.
steps.simpleTranslation: Both of them want it on credit.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that neither side wants advance payment. Both prefer the wages to be paid after the work.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The employer may not have cash ready in advance. The worker prefers to get his money at the end so he doesn't lose it during the day. So payment after the work is normal, and the risk of forgetting remains.

keyTerms.meaning: Credit, payment at a later time.

steps.whatToRemember: The rule exists because a busy employer may forget, and the normal practical ways to avoid that doubt (witnesses or advance payment) don't fit how people actually work.

phrases.english: Both of them want it on credit.
phrases.notes: 'On credit' here just means the worker is paid after the work, not before.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 19.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Paying in advance is a simple fix.
steps.terutzMaskana: Both sides prefer later payment, so the fix isn't used.

steps.title: Then the worker should also swear about the agreed amount
steps.stepSummary: If the בעל הבית may forget, the same should apply when they argue about how much was agreed. Yet a ברייתא says the worker must bring proof.
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, even when they argue about the agreed amount too, the worker should swear and collect! Why then was it taught: A craftsman says, 'You agreed to pay me two,' and the employer says, 'I only agreed to one.' The one who wants to take money from his fellow must bring proof.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tests the 'busy employer' reason against a ברייתא. In that case the worker does not get to swear and collect.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the employer is likely to forget, he could just as easily forget the agreed amount. Yet in a dispute over the amount, the ברייתא applies the normal rule of המוציא מחבירו עליו הראיה, meaning the worker needs proof. So why is forgetting a factor in one case and not the other?

keyTerms.meaning: Whoever wants to take money from another must bring proof.

phrases.english: If so, even when there was a fixed wage too!
phrases.notes: He means: in a dispute about how much was agreed, the worker should also be able to swear and collect.

phrases.english: Why then was it taught in a baraita:
The craftsman says: You fixed two coins for me,
and the other one says:
I only fixed one for you —
the one who takes money from his fellow must bring the proof.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Tests the 'busy employer' reason against a ruling in a ברייתא.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If forgetting is the concern, it should apply to the wage amount too, yet the ברייתא requires proof there.

steps.title: People remember the wage they agreed on
steps.stepSummary: A wage agreement (קציצה) is something people definitely remember, so there is no worry that the employer forgot it.
steps.simpleTranslation: Agreeing on a wage is something people definitely remember.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that forgetting is only a worry about the payment itself, not about the amount agreed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Paying many workers is routine and easy to mix up. Setting the wage is a deliberate, one-time negotiation that sticks in the mind. So with the amount, the normal rule of bringing proof applies.

keyTerms.meaning: Fixing the wage, the wage agreement.

phrases.english: A wage agreement certainly
is something people remember.

steps.triggerLanguage: קְצִיצָה וַדַּאי מִידְכָּר דְּכִירִי לַהּ אִינָשֵׁי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 21 by distinguishing the two cases.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: A busy employer might forget the amount just as he might forget paying.
steps.terutzMaskana: A wage agreement is memorable, so the concern about forgetting doesn't apply to it.

steps.title: Then the worker should also swear after his time has passed
steps.stepSummary: If the בעל הבית may forget, the worker should be able to swear and collect even after the payment time. Yet the משנה says he cannot.
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, even when his time has passed too! Why then did we learn: If his time passed, he does not swear and collect?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tests the 'busy employer' reason against our משנה, which limits the worker's oath to the payment time.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An employer who might forget during the payment time could forget afterward as well. Yet the משנה says that after the time has passed, the worker loses this special right. The 'busy employer' reason doesn't seem to explain that limit.

phrases.aramaic: אִי הָכִי, אֲפִילּוּ עָבַר זְמַנּוֹ נָמֵי,
phrases.english: If so, even when his time has passed too,
why then did we learn:
If his time passed, he does not swear and collect?

steps.triggerLanguage: אִי הָכִי, אֲפִילּוּ עָבַר זְמַנּוֹ נָמֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second test of the 'busy employer' reason, this time against the משנה.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Forgetting could happen after the payment time too, yet the משנה denies the oath then.

steps.title: Employers are presumed not to delay wages
steps.stepSummary: There is a חזקה that a בעל הבית does not violate בל תלין. Once the time has passed, we assume he already paid.
steps.simpleTranslation: There is a presumption that an employer does not violate the prohibition of 'do not delay wages.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that after the payment time, a different factor wins out: we assume the employer would not break the prohibition of holding back wages.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Within the payment time, the employer has not yet done anything wrong, so the worry that he forgot stands. Once the time passes, not paying would mean violating בל תלין. The חזקה that people don't commit that sin is stronger than the worry about forgetting.

keyTerms.meaning: A presumption about how people normally behave.
The prohibition against delaying a worker's wages overnight.

steps.whatToRemember: The שכיר swears and collects within his payment time because a busy employer may have forgotten. That worry does not apply to the agreed amount, which people remember, or after the payment time, when we presume the employer did not violate בל תלין.

phrases.english: There is a presumption: an employer does not violate
the prohibition of 'do not delay wages.'

steps.triggerLanguage: חֲזָקָה: אֵין בַּעַל הַבַּיִת עוֹבֵר מִשּׁוּם בַּל תָּלִין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 23.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The worry that the employer forgot should apply after the payment time too.
steps.terutzMaskana: After the payment time, the חזקה that an employer does not violate בל תלין outweighs the worry that he forgot.

steps.title: But the employer is busy and might forget
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the חזקה from Step 24. It points out that we already said the בעל הבית is busy with his workers and might forget whether he paid.
steps.simpleTranslation: But didn't you say that the employer is busy with his workers?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא objects to the last answer. If the employer is busy and forgets, why do we trust that he paid once the time has passed?
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 24 relied on a חזקה that the בעל הבית keeps בל תלין, so after the deadline we assume he paid. Earlier, though, the גמרא let the worker swear because the employer is busy and may forget. A forgetful employer could think he paid when he did not, even after the deadline, so the two ideas seem to clash.

keyTerms.meaning: But didn't you say. This brings back an earlier statement in order to challenge the current one.

phrases.english: But didn't you say
the employer is busy with his workers!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the חזקה given in Step 24 by setting it against the גמרא's earlier reason that the employer is busy.
steps.kashyaTarget: The חזקה that the בעל הבית does not break בל תלין, so after the deadline we assume he paid.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If the employer's busyness makes him forget, he could wrongly believe he paid even after the deadline. Then the חזקה would not prove that he really paid.

steps.title: Busyness matters only before the payment deadline
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the worry about the employer being busy and forgetting applies only before his payment deadline arrives.
steps.simpleTranslation: That applies only before the time of his obligation to pay arrives.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins its answer by limiting when the 'busy employer' idea applies. The explanation of why this matters continues on the next amud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The two ideas are separated by time. Before the deadline, the employer is busy and may honestly forget whether he paid. Once the deadline arrives, a different factor takes over, and the גמרא is about to explain it.

keyTerms.meaning: This applies only... It is used to limit a rule to a certain case.
The time he becomes obligated to pay, meaning the payment deadline

steps.confusionAlert: Do not read this as saying the employer is never busy after the deadline. The גמרא only says the busyness worry matters before the deadline. The reason it no longer works afterward comes on the next amud.

phrases.english: This applies only
before the time of his obligation arrives,

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers Step 25 by limiting the 'busy employer' reasoning to the time before the payment deadline.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limiting the scope of a principle (חילוק by time)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The employer's busyness would mean he could forget at any time, even after the deadline.
steps.terutzMaskana: The busyness worry applies only before the deadline arrives. After that, the חזקה of not breaking בל תלין takes over, as the next line explains.
